subject: biology
title: Genes, chromosomes and the genetic code
key_idea: A gene is a base sequence of DNA that codes for the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide, or for a functional RNA. DNA is packaged with histones into chromosomes in eukaryotes. The genetic code is triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate and universal.

blocks.text: DNA is stored differently in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. This section covers where it is found and what a gene is.

rows: Chromosomes: a DNA molecule and its histones

items: The DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts is like prokaryotic DNA: short, circular and not associated with protein.
A eukaryotic **chromosome** is one DNA molecule wound around histones, which packages the long molecule into the nucleus.
A **gene** is a base sequence of DNA that codes for the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide, or for a functional RNA such as ribosomal RNA or tRNA.
A gene occupies a fixed position, called a **locus**, on a particular DNA molecule.
Much of the nuclear DNA of eukaryotes does not code for polypeptides.
There are non-coding multiple repeats of base sequences between genes.
Within a gene, **exons** code for amino acid sequences.
Exons are separated by one or more non-coding sequences called **introns**.
Prokaryotes: short circular DNA, no histones. Eukaryotic nucleus: long linear DNA with histones.
A gene codes for a polypeptide or a functional RNA, and has a fixed locus.
Exons code for amino acids; introns do not.

blocks.text: The base sequence of a gene is a code for the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, which is its primary structure.

items: A sequence of three DNA bases, a **triplet**, codes for a specific amino acid.
Some triplets are not amino acids: a start triplet marks where a gene begins and stop triplets mark where it ends.
Three bases per amino acid give 64 possible triplets, which is more than enough for 20 amino acids.

items.meaning: Three bases code for one amino acid.
Each base is part of only one triplet. The code is read in order, three bases at a time.
Most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet.
The same triplets code for the same amino acids in almost all organisms.

items: Because the code is degenerate, a change to one base does not always change the amino acid. This is covered in the note on gene mutations.
Because the code is non-overlapping, adding or removing a base shifts how every later triplet is read.
Because the code is universal, a gene from one species can be read by another, as in genetic engineering.

Different triplets can code for the same amino acid

items: A triplet of bases codes for one amino acid, or marks a start or stop.
Degenerate: more than one triplet per amino acid. Non-overlapping: no shared bases. Universal: same in nearly all organisms.
A gene sets the primary structure of a polypeptide.

checks.q: State three differences between the DNA of a prokaryotic cell and the DNA in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell.
checks.a: Prokaryotic DNA is short and circular and is not associated with proteins. Eukaryotic nuclear DNA is very long and linear and is associated with histones, forming chromosomes.

checks.q: Explain what is meant by a genetic code that is degenerate and non-overlapping.
checks.a: Degenerate: most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet of bases. Non-overlapping: each base is part of only one triplet, so the code is read in separate groups of three.

checks.q: Distinguish between an exon and an intron.
checks.a: An exon is a part of a gene that codes for amino acids. An intron is a non-coding sequence within a gene that separates exons.

items: A gene can code for a functional RNA, including ribosomal RNA and tRNA, as well as for a polypeptide.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts of eukaryotic cells also contain short, circular DNA that is not associated with protein.
In eukaryotes, much nuclear DNA is non-coding, including multiple repeats of base sequences between genes.
A polypeptide is coded for by a gene, which is a sequence of nucleotides forming part of a DNA molecule.
Different triplets of DNA bases either code for specific amino acids or correspond to start and stop codons.
A start codon signals where translation begins, and a stop codon signals that the polypeptide is complete.
Be able to explain how a gene determines the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, which is the primary structure of a protein.
Use all four features of the code: triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate and universal.
